Create Period Labels for a Reporting Tree

Source: R/period_labels_tree.R
period_labels_tree.Rd

Create labels for a reporting tree, in which records are tabulated at different levels of detail: detailed periods, broader periods, and, optionally, period not stated.

Usage

period_labels_tree(
  breaks,
  nodes = NULL,
  open_left = FALSE,
  open_right = FALSE,
  format_single = c("lower", "upper"),
  format_multi = c("at_upper", "below_upper"),
  include_missing = TRUE
)

Arguments

breaks

Boundaries between periods. A numeric vector.

nodes

Labels for broad periods. A character vector, or NULL (the default), in which case there are no broad periods.

open_left

Whether first period is open on the left, i.e. has no lower limit. Default is FALSE.

open_right

Whether last period is open on the right, i.e. has no upper limit. Default is FALSE.

format_single

How to format label for single-year period. Choices are "lower" (the default) and "upper". See below for details.

format_multi

How to format the second number in a label for a multi-year period. With "at_upper" (the default), the second number is the upper limit of the period. With "below_upper", the second number is one year below the upper limit. See below for details.

include_missing

Whether to include a "Missing" category, representing period not stated. Default is TRUE.

Value

Character vector.

Details

The most detailed periods (the leaves of the tree) are created from breaks, open_left, and open_right, exactly as by period_labels(). Broader periods are supplied through nodes, as ordinary period labels. Broader periods can be given in any order, and can nest to any depth. Leaves do not need to be the same distance from the root.

Labels in nodes are interpreted using the same rules as are used to format the leaves, as set by format_single and format_multi. With the default format_multi = "at_upper", for instance, "2000-2010" means the period from the start of 2000 to the start of 2010. Labels in nodes are then converted into the same format as the leaves.

Each broad period must start and end at values in breaks (or be open, if open_left or open_right is TRUE), so that it is a union of detailed periods. It must contain at least two detailed periods, but not all of them, and broad periods must nest: any two either do not overlap, or one contains the other.

The root of the tree, representing records with no information on period, is labelled "Missing". Unlike period_labels(), period_labels_tree() includes "Missing" by default, since most reporting trees in practice have a category for period not stated.

Labels are returned in the same order as period_set_order_tree(): detailed periods, then broad periods (each after the periods inside it), then "Missing".

Rules for formatting output

Single-year periods

format_singleRuleExample
"lower"[a,a+1) -> "a"[2020,2021) -> "2020"
"upper"[a,a+1) -> "<a+1>"[2020,2021) -> "2021"

Multi-year periods

format_multiRuleExample
"at_upper"[a,b) -> "a-b"[2020,2025) -> "2020-2025"
"below_upper"[a,b) -> "a-<b-1>"[2020,2025) -> "2020-2024"

Open periods

Interval typeRuleExample
open on left(-Inf,a) -> "<a"(-Inf,2020) -> "<2020"
open on right[a,Inf) -> "a+"[2020,Inf) -> "2020+"

See also

  • period_labels() Create labels without broad periods

  • period_set_order_tree() Order existing labels as a tree

  • period_diagnose_values() Check labels, including with valid_tree = TRUE

  • age_labels_tree() Age equivalent of period_labels_tree()

  • cohort_labels_tree() Cohort equivalent of period_labels_tree()

Examples

## year of arrival: 5-year periods, a broad group
## for arrivals before 2010, and not stated
period_labels_tree(
  breaks = seq(2000, 2020, 5),
  nodes = "<2010",
  open_left = TRUE
)
#> [1] "<2000"     "2000-2005" "2005-2010" "2010-2015" "2015-2020" "<2010"    
#> [7] "Missing"  

## labels in "below_upper" format
period_labels_tree(
  breaks = seq(2000, 2020, 5),
  nodes = c("2000-2009", "2010-2019"),
  format_multi = "below_upper"
)
#> [1] "2000-2004" "2005-2009" "2010-2014" "2015-2019" "2000-2009" "2010-2019"
#> [7] "Missing"
